mechanisms.causalChain: A regional recession reduces tax bases and nominal GDP while automatic stabilizers, transfers and support raise borrowing; debt/GDP and issuance rise. Higher sovereign yields feed bank, firm and household benchmark costs, with country-specific pass-through shaped by duration, fixed coupons, refinancing needs, fiscal institutions and ECB transmission. Interactions among sovereign risk, bank holdings, credit supply and private demand can reinforce or dampen the initial shock.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Exposure is not uniform and high debt alone does not predict crisis. Euro-area Q2 growth was positive, household consumption contributed positively, and 2026-Q1 ratios were low in some members; maturities, nominal growth, assets, ECB instruments, fiscal capacity and market access can buffer the flow burden. The ECB's September 2026 policy rates remained far below the high-rate stress hypothesized for firms. The ECB’s 2025-Q4 euro-area sector accounts show consolidated NFC debt at 65.8% of GDP, household debt at 50.5% and household debt/income at 81.4%; the broader nonconsolidated NFC ratio is 135.8%. This private-sector balance-sheet context is separate from sovereign gross debt and cautions against treating sovereign ratios as total recession exposure. Q2 2026 ECB accounts now report euro-area NFC debt at 66.0% consolidated (135.6% broader, non-consolidated) and household debt at 80.3% of disposable income; these are euro-area aggregates and revised vintages. ECB SI capital was 16.00% CET1 and EBA EU/EEA CET1 16.1%, with distinct perimeters. BIS Q1 2026 all-sector bank claims on US/China are partial reporter sums, not net or complete exposure; data do not support treating them as full EU financial-sector exposures.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: End-quarter consolidated Maastricht gross debt is a liability stock at face value. The debt ratio evolves with primary balances, effective interest cost, nominal GDP growth, stock-flow adjustments and valuation effects; annual interest cash flow reprices gradually as fixed-rate debt matures and new issuance clears at current yields. Sovereign holdings are also assets on banks' and investors' balance sheets. Debt/GDP is not a measure of gross issuance or near-term refinancing by itself. At the euro-area aggregate level, ECB sector accounts put NFC loans and debt securities at 65.8% of GDP consolidated (135.8% nonconsolidated), and household debt at 50.5% of GDP in 2025-Q4. Creditor-sector holdings and cross-border positions are separate asset-side exposures; avoid adding inter-NFC claims to consolidated liabilities or treating them as sovereign debt. BIS consolidated banking claims provide a partial asset-side channel: in 2026-Q1 immediate-counterparty basis, reported EU27-country reporter sums were USD 69.824bn on China (9/27 available reporters) and USD 2,280.999bn on the US (12/27); guarantor-basis sums were USD 75.740bn (9/27) and USD 2,275.925bn (11/27). These do not reconcile to all-EU totals; suppressed country cells are excluded, never imputed as zero.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Quarterly debt observations are provisional, use trailing four-quarter GDP and may be revised during annual EDP notification. The aggregate hides maturity, holder residency, currency, floating-rate share, off-balance-sheet commitments, public assets and private-sector leverage; one release cannot identify recession causation or spread response. Euro-area composition changed from EA20 to EA21 in 2026, complicating time comparisons. Latest added household/NFC measures are euro-area aggregates, not the full EU or country-matched bank/corporate/household matrix. The ECB 2025-Q4 table gives sector creditor composition, but this work does not produce a matched US-China cross-border exposure matrix or national private-debt maturity/reset ladders; do not imply those have been quantified. The ECB Q2 sector-account data are euro area rather than EU27. SI supervisory measures omit less significant institutions and are not all-EU measures; the full SI+LSI Q2 system release is dated 2026-10-15, after cutoff. EBA EU/EEA and SI perimeters differ. BIS reporting-country totals cover disclosed home-country groups and have uneven/suppressed coverage; no single aggregate should be inferred.
mechanisms.modelability: Model country-level debt dynamics with observed starting debt and GDP, explicit effective interest-rate and maturity ladders, primary balance assumptions, nominal growth and transparent stock-flow adjustments; pass sovereign spreads into bank and private credit through a separately calibrated channel. Avoid treating a single debt/GDP threshold as an insolvency switch.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Relevant to prolonged high rates and combined recession scenarios through fiscal headroom, spread dispersion, countercyclical capacity and monetary transmission. Country heterogeneity means a euro-area average can conceal a sovereign-bank amplification pocket.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Need matched country-level maturity schedules, interest expenditure, foreign/domestic holder composition, gross financing needs, contingent liabilities and bank sovereign exposures at a consistent vintage. Need a defensible shock-to-spread and spread-to-credit elasticity; this evidence bundle does not identify it. At cutoff, full ECB SI+LSI system-wide Q2 publication is pending (scheduled 2026-10-15). Full creditor-country cross-border asset positions, individual bank gross/net exposures, maturity, collateral, hedges and loss-given-default for US/China are not measured by the partial BIS summations; broader non-bank holdings and EU27-wide positions remain unresolved.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The accepted Eurostat release reports Q1 2026 EA21 gross debt at 88.9% of GDP and EU debt at 82.9%, both provisional, and country ratios from 25.2% Estonia to 143.5% Greece; France stood at 117.6%, Italy 138.9%. Debt securities were 84.3% of EA debt. Q2 GDP was +0.6% q/q at the 7 September estimate, but inventories contributed -0.5pp and net exports +0.9pp; the next update was scheduled after this as-of cutoff. Record exposure by country and instrument; do not call the region uniformly fragile or resilient. No core mechanism is retired at this extraction stage. Added ECB 2025-Q4 sector-account data: consolidated NFC debt 65.8% GDP, wider nonconsolidated NFC debt 135.8% GDP, household debt 50.5% GDP and household debt/income 81.4% (period 2025-Q4). These are euro-area-only, not EU-wide and have different consolidation definitions from government debt. End-2024 euro-area general-government debt securities totalled EUR 11,186.3bn; IIP nonresident holdings EUR 2,591.5bn; SHS nonresident stock EUR 2,674.2bn and foreign official holdings EUR 952.4bn. Locator: ECB International Role of the Euro June 2025 report, Table A.1 / printed pp. 39-41. Country-matched sovereign-bank, household, firm, US-China exposure map remains unavailable in this repair. Closure RR0-EU-01 verified ECB Q2 debt release (published 2026-10-02, revised history) and Q2 SI bank release (2026-09-15); EBA EU/EEA dashboard dated 2026-09-25 was used as a separate perimeter check. BIS flat-file data updated 2026-09-14 were filtered to 2026-Q1 EU27 reporter country groups, domestic banks, total claims, all sectors, all instruments/maturities/currencies; only published values were summed. Coverage counts and missing/suppressed reporter codes are retained in closure/bank-sector-exposure-bounds.json/csv.

mechanisms.causalChain: A global or regional shock changes relative expected safety, liquidity, currency and return across assets; foreign investors rebalance euro-area sovereign securities, altering bond demand, yields and spreads. Flow direction differs across countries, maturities, investor types and currencies; ECB purchases/redemptions, hedging costs and domestic institutions can offset or amplify it. Lower sovereign yields may ease bank and corporate funding, while withdrawals can tighten conditions and interact with sovereign-bank holdings.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: ECB's foreign-holdings analysis reports that foreign holdings helped absorb issuance after Eurosystem net purchases stopped, and official foreign holdings remained generally resilient after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the measured decline for non-aligned holders was limited and had very limited yield impact. These observations contradict a simple automatic flight from all euro assets, while also not establishing safe-haven status for every shock. Stabilizing evidence: euro-area foreign official holders were EUR 952.4bn at 2024-Q4 in ECB SHS; foreign holders helped absorb issuance after Eurosystem net purchases ended. ECB research finds post-2021 non-aligned holder decline of EUR 35bn (0.3% of EA debt) and a negligible yield estimate (<1bp) under its symmetry/sample assumptions. These observations are limited to specific episodes and do not imply a safe-haven premium.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: The end-2024 nonresident holding stock (about EUR 2.6tn or 23% of euro-area government debt in the mapped ECB analysis) changes only through gross purchases/sales, issuance/redemption and valuation. A holding share is not a flow. Marginal demand affects auction absorption and secondary-market prices/yields; sovereign yield changes then affect government interest costs over refinancing, collateral valuations and bank portfolios with lags.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Holdings data do not identify investor motive or intraperiod flow; custody locations and beneficial ownership are imperfect, foreign aggregates mix central banks, funds and private investors, and price changes affect values. Historical 2011–12 safe-haven episodes and 2022 geopolitical composition changes do not supply an elasticity for an AI/energy/global-liquidity shock in 2026–30. ECB SHS third-party holder data cover securities with euro-area custodians and can misattribute ultimate ownership through fund/custody chains; the international role report uses Q4 2024 stocks. A historical association between reallocation and spread movement is not a causal estimate for a global AI/high-rate shock. No country-level hedged/unhedged marginal flow response estimated here.
mechanisms.modelability: Represent as scenario-specific, bounded portfolio flow or spread shocks by issuer group and investor class, then pass through transparent sovereign-yield and bank-funding channels. Keep baseline flow at zero absent a measured estimate; explore both stabilizing inflow and reversal cases without labelling either calibrated probability.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Material to the user's relative-anchor hypothesis and EU branch: test whether risk-off demand supports core sovereigns while widening peripheral spreads, and whether safe-haven allocation is offset by risk, currency, energy, fiscal or fragmentation concerns.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: No current high-frequency flow decomposition, hedging-cost sensitivity, beneficial-owner breakdown, sovereign yield response or cross-country substitution elasticity was extracted. Future shocks may change the composition and liquidity premium in ways that past evidence cannot pin down.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: ECB 2025 analysis differentiates foreign total holdings from foreign official holdings, noting official holdings are mainly by non-aligned countries while total foreign holdings are concentrated in geopolitically aligned countries. It reports broadly resilient official holdings since 2022 and small, limited yield impact from the recorded decline in non-aligned holdings. Historical ECB 2012 research covers sovereign-tension reallocations, a context-specific analogue. Treat the 23%/EUR2.6tn stock as exposure context only; do not use it as a forecast of safe-haven flows. Investigate regional core/periphery heterogeneity and currency-hedged versus unhedged demand in subsequent work. No core mechanism is retired. Additional direct ECB evidence confirms aggregate foreign ownership but weakens overgeneralization: Q4 2024 IIP nonresident holdings EUR 2,591.5bn versus SHS EUR 2,674.2bn; SHS foreign official sector EUR 952.4bn, versus total government debt securities EUR 11,186.3bn. ECB 2025 analysis estimates the post-end-2021 non-aligned holdings decline at EUR 35bn (0.3% of euro-area debt) and yield effect below 1bp assuming symmetric equal effects across holder types. This is an ECB staff estimate under specified episode/assumptions, not a future-shock calibration.

mechanisms.causalChain: Import concentration or trade disruption constrains rare-earth feedstock and magnet availability; extraction projects can diversify ore supply only after resource conversion, permitting, financing, construction, recovery and transport. Extraction alone is insufficient without separation/refining, qualified alloy/magnet production and downstream customers. Supply shortfalls can delay EV, wind and electronics production or raise input prices; substitution and inventory drawdowns are partial buffers.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: The CRMA is binding policy with 2030 benchmarks and designated projects, and EU project selections expanded in 2026. LKAB has an existing mining base and reported a large Per Geijer resource while pursuing by-product extraction from existing iron ore. These create credible diversification options, but they do not establish mineable reserves or annual output. The newer project check finds two real downstream processing milestones: Neo reported its Silmet small-scale HREE separation line commissioned and at nameplate in April 2026, producing first Tb/Dy precursor process solutions; Solvay said its La Rochelle permanent-magnet rare-earth line began commercial production in April 2025. Both materially improve the evidence of operational progress, but public tonnes, annual utilization and independent output verification are absent.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Geological resources are in-ground stocks; the relevant economic flow is saleable separated oxide/alloy output per year. Extraction drawdown depends on recovery rate, ore grade, waste, processing capacity, energy/water, permitting, capex, labor, transport and offtake. Inventory buffers and imported concentrates shift timing but do not eliminate dependence; downstream value chains transform oxide into metal, alloy and magnets with yields and losses at each stage.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Company mineral-resource statements are not reserve statements or independent production forecasts. Project timelines and capacities are management plans. Product grades and denominators differ across strategic materials; announced project counts cannot be added into comparable tonnes or benchmark shares. Geopolitical import concentration and substitution elasticities vary by element and end use.
mechanisms.modelability: Model element-specific annual capacity additions as probability-free project states or bounded commissioning schedules, with a distinct extraction-to-separated-oxide yield and an explicit import baseline. Stress delays, utilization and concentration; do not convert resource tonnes directly into yearly output.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: A plausible supply-chain propagation channel under trade fragmentation and a tail stress, relevant to the EU relative-anchor hypothesis as both vulnerability and opportunity for strategic investment. The timing is important: planning and permitting cannot quickly replace a lost major supplier.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Current mine output and trade dependence by element, project-level permits/finance/offtakes, expected grade and recovery, electricity and chemical inputs, and comparable import origin data have not been assembled. Per Geijer reserve conversion and commercial production horizon remain uncertain. The 2026 project register does not supply standardized capacity, financial close, permits, construction completion or annual output data by project; these must be verified project-by-project before modelling supply additions.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The CRMA legal benchmarks approach 10% extraction, 40% processing and 25% recycling of annual Union consumption by 2030, differentiated by strategic raw material and capacity stage. The 2025 and 2026 project rounds evidence pipeline, not commissioning. LKAB's 2023 release reported more than one million tonnes REO as a mineral resource; it explained that resource does not equal reserve and outlined further steps. Its planned Luleå start date is a forward plan, not observation. LKAB states current EU permanent-magnet import dependence is high, but that company statement should be triangulated with official trade statistics before calibration. No mechanism retired. The official Commission live register confirms a second 2026 selection wave: 46 projects across 16 Member States, in addition to the first EU wave; designations broaden the pipeline but are not capacity additions until permitting, financing, construction, commissioning, feed and customer qualification are complete. The Per Geijer resource remains a geological stock: LKAB itself describes resource classification and a long permitting/mining path; its 2023 estimate is not annual extractable REO flow.  Estonia is not only Narva magnet manufacture: Neo’s 2026-04-10 company release reports a distinct Silmet small-scale heavy-REE solvent extraction line commissioned at nameplate, first separated Tb/Dy process solutions from mixed carbonate feed, with product purity still being stabilized. No nameplate volume or tonnes produced is given. Swedish LKAB FY2025 annual report was checked; Per Geijer remains a project/resource rather than current mine output, and no commercially verified rare-earth annual saleable flow/cost series was extracted. Project economics (energy, reagents, recovery, feed, offtake, prices) remain unavailable publicly in a comparable audited form.

mechanisms.causalChain: Even if mined or recycled material exists, separation and refining bottlenecks can constrain usable rare-earth oxides; alloy and magnet manufacturing then require process qualification, scale, energy, chemicals, technical labor and customer certification. A plant's commissioning/ramp and utilization determine the flow that can substitute for imports. Capacity shortfalls can create input scarcity, higher costs, delayed production and weak returns that in turn threaten project financing.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: Narva's European magnet plant opened in 2025 and a 2026 government-investment page reported commercial magnet production and shipments; Caremag disclosed secured project financing and named planned feed/output capacities. The pipeline therefore has realized milestone progress, though milestone evidence does not quantify full-year throughput or upstream independence. Revised evidence includes Silmet’s operating small-scale HREE solvent extraction line (first Tb/Dy process solutions; purity stabilization ongoing) and Solvay’s La Rochelle commercial-start announcement for a permanent-magnet rare-earth line in 2025. This confirms stage-specific operation/launch milestones, not rated annual tonnes or sustained production.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Nameplate capacity is an installed/design flow ceiling, not actual production. Annual saleable output equals capacity multiplied by commissioning, utilization, process yield, feed availability and product qualification. Caremag's 2,000 tonnes/year of magnet feed and 5,000 tonnes/year concentrate feed are distinct input streams; oxide output is another stage and cannot be added to magnet capacity. Narva magnet tonnes are downstream manufacturing, not EU mining or separation capacity.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Most project evidence is company or investment-promotion disclosure; no audited 2026 throughput, utilization, full feedstock origin or independently verified yield series is in the map. Project descriptions may be updated and planned expansion is not installed output. CRMA project selection does not certify completion. Cross-facility capacities may overlap or use different materials and units.
mechanisms.modelability: Build a plant-by-plant stage table with observed status (announced, funded, construction, commissioning, qualified commercial production), input/output unit, rated capacity and start date. Use utilization/ramp assumptions explicitly and range them; apply yield and feed constraints. Count production only when independently supported for observed years.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Refining capacity determines how quickly EU supply can respond to import interruption and whether recycling projects actually reduce upstream dependency. Local capacity may still rely on imported concentrate, and output may be committed through offtake elsewhere.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Missing audited ramp/utilization, customer qualification, material composition, feed origin, capacity change at Narva, and Caremag commissioning status/output by cutoff. Need technical boundaries between separation, refining, alloy and magnet production before material-flow model is parameterized. As-of-cutoff verification found no audited full-year Narva output or Caremag commissioning, throughput, yield or utilization. Capacity figures are company design claims and refer to different stages/streams. Silmet release omits small-scale nameplate tonnes, post-commissioning stable purity, routine production, yield, cost and input provenance. Solvay release states commercial production and a 30% European-demand objective but no annual output, utilization, feed split, economics or denominator; do not translate either milestone into EU supply volumes.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: Accepted map provides 2025 Neo Narva opening, a 2024 annual information form with planned Phase 1 nameplate capacity of 2,000 tonnes/year and contemplated later 5,000 tonnes/year, and a 2026 Invest in Estonia report of commercial production and shipments without observed annual volumes; exact page publication date is undisclosed and remains null. Caremag's 17 March 2025 release reported €216m secured financing, design feed of 2,000 tonnes/year magnets and 5,000 tonnes/year concentrates, plus planned oxide outputs; its late-2026 operations date remains a plan at cutoff. Distinguish capacity by value-chain stage and do not claim observed annual output. No mechanism retired. By 2026, Neo/Invest in Estonia reports Narva commercial supply to an EV traction-motor Tier 1 customer, but it reports no tonnes/year. Neo reported in 2025 that production/shipment of qualification samples began and that the facility was operational since May 2025; this progression is credible milestone evidence, not utilization. Carester’s 2026-04-09 update still scheduled Caremag commissioning for late 2026 and gives 2,000 t/y magnet feed and 5,000 t/y concentrate feed as design input streams. It did not report that commissioning had occurred by the 2026-10-14 cutoff.  Add a clear stage distinction: Silmet (Sillamäe) is separation/refining; Narva is downstream magnet manufacture. Neo’s April 2026 release reports HREE line commissioning/nameplate operation at an undisclosed small-scale capacity and first Tb/Dy precursor solutions; purity was still being stabilized. Solvay’s April 2025 source says La Rochelle’s magnet-material line began commercial production. Public disclosure does not provide independently auditable tonnage or plant economics for either. LKAB report checked: Per Geijer resource/possible later development remains upstream potential, not operational annual REO. Caremag remains planned/financed feed capacity with commissioning scheduled late-2026 in latest dated 2026 update; no audited cutoff production located.

mechanisms.causalChain: Permanent magnets embedded in vehicles, turbines, appliances and equipment enter the in-use stock for years; product lifetime, collection, disassembly and sorting determine when and how much magnet scrap becomes feed. Recovery and separation yields determine secondary rare-earth output; demand can grow faster than this lagged waste flow, so new recycling plants may initially compete for limited feedstock. Recycling can reduce virgin imports over time but cannot be inferred from generic waste recycling rates or nameplate capacity.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: The Commission identifies <1% EU rare-earth recycling and also reports that Carester, Solvay and Inspiree could contribute about 3,800 tonnes of rare-earth permanent magnets, around 20% of then-current demand, in coming years if feedstock and incentives are in place. This supports potential material contribution; it is a conditional projection, not a realized end-of-life input rate. Manufacturing scrap and imported secondary material may provide additional feed beyond retired EU products if correctly traced. Solvay’s 2025 primary press release does state a corporate objective of meeting 30% of European rare-earth demand by 2030 and reports the La Rochelle line’s commercial start; it does not attribute that objective to recycling alone, give a demand denominator or report achieved output. This likely creates/echoes ambiguity with the alleged ~30% recycling-sufficiency claim; it cannot replace the missing mass balance. The available CEPS cohort model provides source-linked scenario bounds: selected-application secondary supply equals 8-19% of demand in 2025-2030, 16-34% in 2040 and 24-48% in 2050. These challenge a precise 30% claim but remain scenario outputs, not observed throughput or probabilities; the 2030 theoretical EOL availability is about 10 kt against 36 kt modeled selected-application demand.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: The end-of-life stream is a delayed function of historic sales/installation cohorts, product magnet intensity, trade, lifespan and collection share. Available feed is not the same as recoverable material; multiply by sorting/disassembly capture, magnet recovery, separation/refining yield and quality acceptance. Secondary material flow then displaces a share of primary feed, subject to demand growth, export/import flows and stock accumulation. CRMA's 25% capacity benchmark has a different numerator and denominator from recycled input actually consumed. Cohort turnover delays feed: the CEPS model uses 13-year EV, 12-year conventional vehicle, 25-year onshore wind and 30-year offshore wind lives, with collection/dismantling scenarios by application. For EVs, the table uses 50/90% collection and 85/95% dismantling scenario rates; reported first large EV retirements begin around 2035, with roughly 10 kt/y of EV EOL magnet material by 2040. Manufacturing scrap is not in this EOL flow model. Do not equate magnet mass, contained element, oxide, metal or separated magnet output.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: EU-wide permanent-magnet dynamic material-flow series is not established by the accepted map. JRC methodology warns generic EOL recycling input and EOL recycling efficiency differ; JRC wind turbine projections cover one product stock and the UK study is not an EU estimate. Commission capacity projections rely on feedstock/incentive conditions. Recovery rates, trade in scrap and product-specific magnet content remain data gaps. CEPS model covers selected applications (about 68% of the overall magnet market in its 2020 estimate) and uses projected EV sales, assumed lifetimes and collection/disassembly, so its denominator and supply shares are incomplete scenarios. It does not establish actual current utilization, universal refining/recycling yield, plant feed economics, manufacturing-scrap flow, or complete Pr/Tb demand. JRC 2026 wind outflow is an element outflow estimate with lifetime sensitivity, not recycled production.
mechanisms.modelability: Use cohort-based material-flow accounting by application, with annual additions, import/export, magnet intensity, service life distributions, collection, disassembly and process yields. Reconcile physical inputs and outputs by material and stage, cap secondary production by available scrap, and scenario-test faster collection or substitution without assuming immediate end-of-life feed. Bounded scenario mass accounting is possible for selected cohorts using the CEPS demand/TRP and chain-level secondary-supply shares; keep its coverage and assumptions visible. Plant throughput, scrap and element-specific separated-oxide/metal yields should remain unknown parameters or explicit scenario assumptions rather than calibrated observations.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Tests EU resilience claims and supply-chain adaptation over 2026–30. Short-run recycling is constrained by in-use stocks; medium/longer-run contribution can grow as installed EV and wind cohorts retire. This changes the time profile of import dependence, not simply the long-run target value. The evidence supplies plausible low/high supply-share envelopes (8-19% 2025-30, 16-34% 2040, 24-48% 2050) and a cohort lag useful for stress scenarios; it cannot justify a deterministic 30% recycling supply baseline.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Need EU magnet demand by element/use, existing stock cohorts, product lifetime curves, collection and exports, manufacturing-scrap share, current plant feed contracts and process yields. The alleged ~30% sufficiency claim is not evidenced by this source set and cannot be confirmed or rejected quantitatively without matched demand and feedstock accounting. The source of a round 30% figure may be Solvay’s company objective; scope is rare-earth demand and planned production, not demonstrated recycled magnets as a share of EU demand. No public matched tonne denominator, supply split, output or recycling share is supplied. EU product-cohort stock, retirements, collection/export, scrap, yields and demand remain unassembled. No source-located aggregate EU manufacturing-scrap quantity, complete Nd/Pr/Dy/Tb magnet stock composition, plant-specific feedstock availability, commercial yields, or audited Caremag/Solvay/Silmet throughput was identified. Data remain absent or private, not zero. Caremag’s 2 kt/y used-magnet input and 5 kt/y concentrate input are separate planned streams; the latter is not recycled magnet feed. Neo Silmet HREE line throughput is undisclosed; Narva is downstream magnet-block manufacture. Solvay’s 30% is an objective with no identified denominator/output observation.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The 2025 RESOurceEU communication says <1% of rare-earth elements are recycled in the EU and conditionally anticipates roughly 3,800 t of permanent magnets (~20% of then-current demand) from Carester/Solvay/Inspiree as projects ramp. Those tonnes and shares are not the CRMA's 25% capacity benchmark, and neither is an observed recycled-input ratio. Caremag feed capacities and oxide output belong to separate mass-flow stages. JRC wind report models slow growth in end-of-life turbine streams through 2030 and larger streams later, while excluding repowering in conservative cases; it covers wind only. JRC system analysis defines distinct EOL recycling indicators; UK MFA is useful for stock/lifetime structure but not EU numerical calibration. Conduct a mass-balance investigation before making a sufficiency claim. No mechanism retired. Caremag’s announced 2,000 t/y magnet feed is an input capacity, not 2,000 t/y of rare-earth oxide or EU end-of-life recycled content. Its separate 5,000 t/y concentrate feed is primary mining concentrate. The announced oxide outputs are another stage. Carester’s own 2026 schedule remained future commissioning as of the cutoff. CRMA 25% is a strategic-raw-material recycling-capacity benchmark, not a permanent-magnet share of demand. Thus the alleged ~30% sufficiency cannot be inferred; its denominator, material, scope (manufacturing scrap vs end-of-life) and annual feed availability must be specified. Corrected JRC citation: JRC112720 (2018-11-20), not JRC125101; the latter is a 2021 report on nine different materials and is registered separately as a citation audit. The Solvay April 2025 release begins La Rochelle commercial production and says its first step is an objective of satisfying 30% of European rare-earth demand by 2030; this is a company goal, not an observed 30% contribution and not specifically a recycled-magnet share. It reports no tonnes/year or matched denominator. The alleged figure therefore remains unsubstantiated as recycling sufficiency, with an identified possible source of confusion. Closure RR0-EU-01 added CEPS Rizos et al. 2022 report extraction at PDF pp.30-32, 37-44 and cross-checked JRC permanent-magnet and wind studies. A transparent bounded selected-application mass-balance table and CSV are at closure/magnet-mass-balance.json/csv. It distinguishes observed/announced capacity stages and separates ore/concentrate, separated oxides/solutions, metal/magnet and EOL feed. No exact 30% sufficiency conclusion is made.

mechanisms.causalChain: Automotive CO2 rules and fleet compliance periods alter manufacturers' product mix, investment timing, emissions-credit needs and demand for battery, hybrid and combustion technologies. An enacted target or amendment changes binding constraints; Commission proposals and Council working documents do not. Misstating a proposal as an adopted hybrid exception would distort transition-path assumptions for auto demand, investment, critical-material requirements and supply-chain cash flows.
mechanisms.counterEvidence: The law includes a 2026 review clause explicitly considering technological development including plug-in hybrids, and the Commission's 2025 proposal would allow 10% of the 2035 tailpipe reduction to be compensated by specified low-carbon steel/e-fuels/biofuels. Future legislative amendments remain possible; this is a live policy process, not proof that hybrid technology was excluded permanently.
mechanisms.stockFlowTransmission: Regulation affects future model development, factory capex and fleet sales rather than immediately changing the installed vehicle stock. Compliance averaging can shift manufacturer credit needs and sales timing over 2025–27. A new adopted post-2035 flexibility measure would alter future production and magnet/battery demand only through product choices, rollout, fleet turnover and consumer adoption; an unadopted proposal has no binding balance-sheet obligation change.
mechanisms.identificationLimits: Policy status must be checked against final Official Journal text and legislative stage, not political announcements or secondary press. Accepted map's June 2026 Council progress report describes divergent member-state views, not adoption. No verified March 2026 agreement record is present; source absence in this map cannot alone prove no external political event, so phrase as not verified and verify legislative tracker before final publication.
mechanisms.modelability: Encode enacted law as baseline legal constraints; encode proposals as alternate policy branches with an adoption-date switch and uncertain behavioral response. Avoid translating percentage tailpipe targets directly into hybrid sales shares; use technology costs, consumer demand, compliance flexibility and turnover assumptions separately.
mechanisms.scenarioRelevance: Relevant to EU auto manufacturing, investment and critical-mineral demand scenarios. A genuine enacted hybrid flexibility could alter near-term transition capex and rare-earth magnet demand, while legal uncertainty itself can defer investment. It has little bearing on sovereign safe-haven status absent a macro/industry scale bridge.
mechanisms.unresolvedUncertainty: Need current EUR-Lex procedure status and any post-June 2026 legislative actions at the 14 October cutoff; exact identity of the claimed March 2026 'hybrid automobile deal'; manufacturer-specific technology and fleet responses; interaction with review and implementation rules. The exact source of the alleged March “hybrid agreement” is unidentified, so the finding is absence of an identified EU-wide hybrid legislative agreement in the checked primary records, not a claim that no national announcement or unrelated vehicle agreement occurred.
mechanisms.investigationNotes: The accepted map distinguishes (1) Regulation 2023/851, binding 2035 100% reduction target from 2021 with 2026 review clause; (2) 2025 adopted compliance averaging for 2025–27; (3) Commission Automotive Package of 16 Dec 2025 proposal for 90% tailpipe reduction plus specified compensation; and (4) June 2026 Council progress report with divergent positions and no adoption. These are not interchangeable. No primary record in this map substantiates a March 2026 hybrid deal. Present the assertion as unverified, do a final current legal tracker check before public-facing claims, and do not treat proposals as law. No mechanism retired. Fresh cutoff check of EUR-Lex procedure 2025/0420/COD reports the Commission’s COM(2025)995 proposal as ongoing on 2026-10-14. The 17 March Environment Council held a policy debate; the 25 June Council took stock of negotiations and outstanding items.
